Design Problem Response

# **"DeepRead"— helps you "understand" complex content.**

## Yi Fan（Spike）S4106162

![][image1]

Figure 1 : Edge browser's exploration and development of the Immersive Reading feature

# **Project Introduction**

My daily reading is quite varied—course papers, technical blogs, lab literature, and long articles retweeted on Twitter. But as I read, I realized I was constantly "switching modes": sometimes I just wanted to glance at the conclusion, sometimes I needed to understand the reasoning, and sometimes I couldn't understand the terminology and had to find an analogy to continue. In different scenarios, "finishing reading" and "understanding" are completely different things.

# **I. Project Overview and Core Themes**

\*\*Project Name:\*\* DeepRead 

\*\*Project Format:\*\* Browser Extension

\*\*Theme:\*\* How to regain control of in-depth reading in the era of AI summarization

\*\*Technology Stack:\*\*HTML5 / CSS3 / JavaScript, Browser Extension API, @mozilla/readability, D3.js / Mermaid.js, LLM API

The motivation behind this project is very personal. As a student, you have to switch between course papers, technical documents, and news reports every day. I've found my reading style is turning into a 'sprint': when I encounter a difficult or long article, I let the AI summarize it; when I see code I don't understand, I ask it directly; when I come across a long report, I scroll through frantically to find conclusions and opinions. Efficiency has indeed improved, but I'm increasingly uncertain—did I really "understand" these things, or was I just collecting a bunch of algorithmically preprocessed fragments?

In an era where AI can sum up everything for us, is "reading" itself being redefined? Maryanne Wolf (2018) reminds us in *《Reader, Come Home》* that deep reading is not just about acquiring information; it also trains reasoning, analogy, critical analysis, and empathy. We are living in an era of "endless reading"; when information exceeds processing capacity, the quality of human decisions and the depth of understanding significantly decline. What we face is no longer "not being able to find information," but rather "finding it but not finishing, not understanding, and not remembering."

It's not anyone's fault. It's just that our brains haven't kept up with the speed of information explosion, while tools are still busy "giving more," not "helping deeper"Eppler and Mengis (2004). 

# **II. Why does this problem need to be solved ?**

### **Existing solutions all have gaps.**

Reading aids on the market can generally be divided into two categories.

The first category is summarization tools (such as TL; DR, Summarly), they excel at "shortening long articles." But the problem is—the summary tells you "what the conclusion is," but not "how did this conclusion come about?" If you only remember the conclusion but don't know the argumentation process, you actually don't truly understand—you're just told the answer.

The second category is more comprehensive reading comprehension tools, such as Readwise Reader and Kagi Summarizer, which break down key points in the sidebar. However, these tools are positioned more like "efficiency tools," assuming users' core needs are "faster access to information" rather than "better understanding information."

Figure 2 : The core functionality of the summarization tool TL;DR

I used to think that "reading fast" meant "high efficiency," but I later realized that's not the case. I once used AI to skim the summary and conclusion of a design document in three minutes, but during the discussion, when someone asked me, "How was it validated in the design?", I could only mechanically repeat the summary the AI ​​gave me. After that, I realized: what truly held me back wasn't speed, but whether I had truly grasped the logic of the article. Good tools shouldn't make judgments for me, but rather let me choose—this one I need to speed read, that one I need to slowly digest.

### **The neglected "cognitive autonomy"**

When you ask AI to help you summarize an article, you are essentially handing over the judgment of "what's important and what's not" to the AI. If AI hides certain information by default, you might not even know what you're missing (Peng et al. 2026\) .

Text algorithms have never been neutral—they are inherently prone to selection. Even seemingly neutral text algorithms can develop systematic selection biases due to biases in training data. Gerdon et al. (2022) If a summarization tool always emphasizes one type of argument and ignores another, over time, your judgment framework will subtly become misguided.

"DeepRead" wants to try something on this issue—not by "avoiding AI" to avoid risks, but by making the AI's workflow transparent and visible. The tree diagram shows the argument structure to tell the user: "This is how AI interprets the logic of this article. You judge for yourself whether it's correct." The point of controversy is meant: "There may be another explanation here; I suggest you read the original text yourself." "

# **III. Different Forms of Design Patterns**

### **Highlight text content** 

Figure 3 :A text-based AI assistant (Lex.page)

Lex.page turns the AI writing assistant into an "on-call" team member. By highlighting text \+ @lex and asking questions directly, users can request local polishing, style transformation, language modifications, and other operations without interrupting the writing process.

**Two core AI-UX patterns:**

* Human in the loop — AI only acts within the text range selected by the user, and every request is user-initiated Amershi et al. (2019) .

* User curation — AI provides suggestions, but the user decides whether to accept, modify, or dismiss them.

**User Intention**

* Quickly optimize sentences or paragraphs in long-form writing.  
* Specify tone and style, such as "Make this more conversational."  
* Rewrite the expression while maintaining semantics.  
* Refine the content through multiple rounds of interaction.

Lex.page's interaction design is noteworthy because it compresses AI collaboration into the context of text selection. Users highlight a paragraph and enter a @lex to complete the AI call—no need to jump to the interface, copy and paste prompts, or even remember any commands. Then, users can directly issue commands in everyday language, such as "Make this more casual," and AI can understand and generate the corresponding rewritten version. Throughout the process, users always hold the initiative: the AI's returned results can directly replace the original text, or it can continue to ask questions and iterate and make changes, forming a natural chain of contextual dialogue. The most subtle detail of the entire interaction is that the AI responds only with "writing..." Lightweight prompts prevent pop-ups and don't steal keyboard focus, maximizing the smoothness of writing.

When AI is light enough, close enough, and obedient enough, users' trust in it increases significantly, and they may even be willing to repeatedly engage in conversations with it within the same document until they produce a version they are satisfied with. This shift from "one-time Q\&A" to "continuous collaboration" is the truly deserving direction for AI-text collaboration to explore. And this was exactly the starting point I started when designing the "Deep Read" plugin: reading and writing, like writing, don't need a substitute, but a transparent assistant who is always on call and leaves you with the right to decide.

# **IV. Design Concept and Implementation Path**

### **Design Rationale**

Turning Deep Read into a browser extension is my understanding of "How AI Should Intervene in Reading."

The biggest advantage of the extension is that it does not alter the original website, but only overlays a reading interface on the original page. This means I have set a premise: that the original webpage is "correct," and Deep Read is just an auxiliary perspective, not pretending to be more correct than the original. Users can turn it off at any time and return to the original page—the opt-out  is the restraint I hope this tool always maintains.

Another core consideration is the scenario. Users' reading behavior naturally occurs within the browser—searching for information, reading papers, scrolling through long articles, all completed in the same window. The extension is the most natural entry point in these scenarios. There is no need to copy links, paste them into another app and wait for it to load; the context of reading is preserved from the very beginning.

Figure 4 : Architectural overview of the WebKit plugin infrastructure. 

For me, the extension is a suitable scope. I have some development experience with it, and it does not require me to build a complete reading platform; it only needs to focus on one thing: proving that the core interaction is feasible and worth using.

### **Design Concept**

DeepRead's core goal is clear: to help users read more clearly. Around this goal, I envisioned three functions that work together with each other.

The first is "Introduction and Structure Tree," which helps you understand "what the article is about and how it is said." When users open any article—whether news, blogs, technical documents, or academic papers—clicking the plugin icon will first display three guided passages: the first summarizes the article's theme, the second extracts the author's core viewpoints, and the third explains what value the article might offer to current users. Below the introduction is an interactive argumentation tree diagram presenting the article's logical framework in a hierarchical structure: top-level nodes are the core argument, sub-nodes are supporting evidence, and leaf nodes are specific data or references. The tree diagram supports folding and expansion. Clicking any node will automatically scroll the main page to the corresponding original paragraph.

The second feature, "Plain Explanation," targets the most common reading stucks: obscure technical terms, complex formulas, and unfamiliar code snippets. When users select such content, hovering or clicking triggers the AI to rephrase what it is doing in plain language, accompanied by a life-like analogy—for example, "This algorithm is similar to the classification logic used when organizing library books."

The third feature, "Controversy Point Annotation," is an optional critical reading aid. While analyzing the article, the AI simultaneously identifies potentially controversial, insufficiently evidence-based, or implicitly positioned sections, summarizes and displays them under the "Points of Dispute" tab at the bottom of the sidebar, and lightly marks the corresponding points on the main page—marking content sufficiently restrained without disrupting the reading rhythm of the main text. Users can enable or disable this feature at any time as needed.

I've gone through several versions of the order for these three features. Initially, I wanted to put "Controversial Annotation" first because I'm most concerned about the article's stance. But then I realized that if users don't even understand what the article is about, annotating it as controversial is pointless. So, I finally settled on the current order—first providing the overall picture, then clearing away obstacles, and finally reminding you "this part may be controversial." Each function actually answers the initial question: how to shift reading from "passive receiving of information" to "actively constructing understanding."

![][image2]

Figure 5: DeepRead System Architecture and Data Flow

The DeepRead system workflow is divided into three layers: extraction layer, analysis layer, and interaction layer. After users click the plugin icon, Readability extracts the main text and passes it to the LLM API to generate a guide, tree diagram, and controversial point annotation, which is then rendered and displayed in the sidebar. The plain explanation function adopts an "on-demand trigger" model, where users select content before initiating API calls, avoiding unnecessary requests. Node clicks in the tree diagram only trigger frontend scrolling behavior and do not involve backend communication.

# **V. Design Summary and Future Vision**

DeepRead's starting point is simple: in a world where AI can read everything for us, do we still want to read for ourselves—and if so, how?

DeepRead isn't another summarization tool. It's more like a transparent reference layer that sits alongside your reading—an introduction and a structure tree help you see the big picture, plain-language explanations clear technical hurdles, and controversy markers remind you when something might need a second look. 

Of course, this is only an early exploration. The accuracy of the structure tree and the false-positive rate of controversy detection still depend on the underlying LLM; whether these features actually deepen comprehension still needs testing and iteration over the course of the semester. But I don't want to stop at asking whether users "like it." The shift from paper to screens once prompted a wave of reflection on whether reading itself was changing. But today, AI summarization has been quietly baked into browser results, email digests, and everyday tools—without us ever really asking what it means to move from electronic reading to AI-assisted reading (Sorin Adam Matei 2013\) .

From the initial conception of this project until now, I can't guarantee that "using DeepRead will definitely lead to deeper reading." But one change is certain: before, when I used AI to read things, what I submitted was a bunch of "processed fragments"; now, I can see how the AI ​​breaks down the article, which parts it deems problematic, and which parts it replaces with plain language. I may not agree with it every time, but at least I know what it did. This alone is a significant improvement for me compared to before.

# **VI. AI Usage**

This assignment utilized the DeepSeek V4 model (July 30 – August 7, 2026\) during the topic selection and language polishing stages. I guided the AI ​​through multiple rounds of questioning to challenge and supplement the initial framework, assisting in the translation of key concepts in foreign language literature, and optimizing the logical connections and sentence structure of some paragraphs. The AI ​​output is only for reference and as a language tool; all content has undergone secondary review and substantial rewriting by myself, and I am solely responsible for its content.
